title: Advent: The Christmas Story
intro: The Christmas story through the days of Advent, from the prophets' promises to the night in Bethlehem.

posts.display: If only You would rend the heavens and come down, so that mountains would quake at Your presence.
posts.caption: Advent comes from the Latin adventus, meaning "coming." It's the season of the four Sundays before Christmas, and today is the first, when many churches light the first candle of an Advent wreath, often for hope. Starting today, 27 days through the Christmas story. It begins with longing: this prayer from late in Isaiah asks God to break into a troubled world.

In the 730s BC, King Ahaz of Judah was terrified of an attack by two neighboring kings. The prophet Isaiah offers him a sign: a child called Immanuel, Hebrew for "God with us." The Hebrew word almah means a young woman; the ancient Greek translation reads "virgin." Jewish readers often see the sign fulfilled in Isaiah's own day, while Christians read it as pointing to Jesus.

The northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, around Galilee, had been overrun by the Assyrian empire, and 2 Kings 15 records their people being taken captive. Into that gloom, Isaiah promises a great light. Centuries later, Matthew's Gospel quotes this passage when Jesus begins his work in Galilee.

The light Isaiah promised arrives as a royal child. His titles describe an ideal king from David's line, and "Prince of Peace" became one of the best-known Christian names for Jesus. Jewish tradition has often read the child as King Hezekiah, Ahaz's son. Handel set this verse to music in his oratorio Messiah, first performed in 1742.

Jesse was the father of King David. Isaiah pictures David's royal family tree cut down to a stump, with a new shoot growing from its roots: a future king who would rule with wisdom and justice. The image inspired the "Tree of Jesse" in medieval art, and the Advent custom of a Jesse tree, hung with ornaments for the stories leading up to Jesus.

About a century after Isaiah, the prophet Jeremiah watched Judah's last kings fail as Babylon closed in. He repeats the promise with a similar image: a "righteous Branch" for David, a king who would finally rule with justice. The prophet Zechariah later uses "the Branch" almost as a name for this hoped-for king.

Micah, who prophesied around the same time as Isaiah, names a small town: Bethlehem, a few miles south of Jerusalem and the hometown of King David. Ephrathah was an old name for the clan and area around it. A new ruler for Israel would come from the same humble place David did. Matthew's Gospel later quotes this verse.

The second Sunday of Advent, when many churches light a second candle, often for peace. Isaiah 40 opens with "Comfort, comfort My people," words to Jewish exiles in Babylon, and promises a road home through the desert with God leading the way. All four Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus.

In most Christian Bibles, Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, so this promise sits just before the Gospels begin. God says a messenger will come first to prepare the way, and Malachi later names him as the prophet Elijah. Many Jewish families still set out a cup for Elijah at the Passover meal. Luke's Gospel opens with an angel promising a child who will come in Elijah's spirit.

Luke's Gospel opens in the temple in Jerusalem. An elderly priest named Zechariah has been chosen by lot to burn incense, a rare honor, when an angel appears beside the altar. He and his wife Elizabeth had grown old without children. The name John comes from the Hebrew Yochanan, meaning "the LORD has been gracious."

In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy, the same angel, Gabriel, is sent to Nazareth, a small village in Galilee. He comes to Mary, who is engaged to Joseph, a descendant of King David. In its old Latin form, "Hail, full of grace," Gabriel's greeting became the opening of the Hail Mary, a prayer central to Catholic devotion.

Gabriel tells Mary she will have a son named Jesus, and describes him in royal terms. About a thousand years earlier, according to 2 Samuel 7, God promised King David that his throne would last forever. By Mary's time, no descendant of David had been king for nearly 600 years, so Gabriel's words revive that old promise.

Mary had asked how this could happen, since she was a virgin. Gabriel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her, adding that "no word from God will ever fail." This is her reply, often called her fiat, from the Latin for "let it be." The scene is known as the Annunciation, and it has been a favorite subject of painters for centuries.

Mary hurries to the hill country of Judah to visit her relative Elizabeth, now about six months pregnant. As soon as Mary arrives, Elizabeth's unborn son, the future John the Baptist, leaps. Together with Gabriel's greeting, Elizabeth's words form the first part of the Hail Mary prayer. This meeting is known as the Visitation.

The third Sunday of Advent is traditionally called Gaudete Sunday, from the Latin for "rejoice," and in many churches today's candle is rose-colored, for joy. Fittingly, this is the start of Mary's song of joy. It's called the Magnificat, the first word of its Latin version, and for centuries it has been sung daily at evening prayer in many churches.

Mary's song turns the usual order of the world upside down: rulers fall, the humble are lifted up, the hungry are fed. It closely echoes the song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2, sung by another woman after God gave her a son. In Greek, Mary's verbs are in the past tense, as if God's great reversal has already happened.

Elizabeth gives birth to a son. On the eighth day, family and neighbors gather for his circumcision, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, and expect him to be named after his father. Elizabeth says no. Zechariah, unable to speak since the angel's visit, asks for a writing tablet and settles it, and in the next verse his voice returns.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zechariah sings. His song is called the Benedictus, from its first Latin word, "Blessed," and is sung at morning prayer in many churches. It ends by picturing the Messiah as sunrise: "the Dawn will visit us from on high." The Greek word for Dawn, anatole, is the same word the ancient Greek Old Testament used for Jeremiah's "Branch."

Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side. In Jewish custom of the time, a betrothal was a binding agreement, and ending it required a formal divorce. Finding that Mary is pregnant, Joseph decides to end things quietly rather than expose her to public shame. From today until December 23, many churches sing the "O Antiphons," the centuries-old prayers behind the hymn "O Come, O Come, Emmanuel."

Before Joseph can act, an angel speaks to him in a dream. Joseph is guided by dreams several times in Matthew's opening chapters, much like his namesake in Genesis, the famous dreamer. Matthew even lists this Joseph's father as Jacob, the name of the Genesis Joseph's father. "Son of David" points back to the royal family tree that opens the chapter.

The angel tells Joseph what to name the child. Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yeshua (Joshua), which means "the LORD saves," so the angel's explanation plays on the name itself. It was a common name at the time. Many scholars note that by naming the child, Joseph takes him as his own legal son.

The fourth Sunday of Advent, when the last of the four candles on many Advent wreaths is lit, often for love. Matthew quotes Isaiah's sign to King Ahaz from earlier in this plan, and translates Immanuel for his readers. The idea frames his whole Gospel, which ends with Jesus saying, "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20).

Luke sets the story on a world stage. Augustus, the first Roman emperor, ruled from 27 BC to 14 AD, and an inscription from his time hails his birthday as the beginning of "good news" for the world. Luke's census has long puzzled historians, since the best-known census under Quirinius (next verse) was around 6 AD, and scholars still debate how the dates fit.

Joseph travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the small town Micah had named centuries earlier, because he belongs to David's family line. Bethlehem means "house of bread" in Hebrew. The journey would have taken several days on foot. Luke never mentions a donkey; that familiar detail comes from later tradition.

Mary, now pregnant, travels with Joseph. Luke says only that the time came "while they were there." He doesn't describe a frantic search on the night they arrived, as many Christmas plays do, and they may have been in Bethlehem for some time. Christmas is now two days away.

Christmas Eve, and the story reaches the birth itself. Newborns were commonly wrapped snugly in strips of cloth, and a manger is a feeding trough for animals. The Greek word translated "inn," kataluma, can also mean a guest room (Luke uses it for the room of the Last Supper), so many scholars picture a crowded family home with animals kept close by.

Merry Christmas. In the fields near Bethlehem, where young David once kept his father's sheep, shepherds were keeping watch by night when an angel appeared with this news. "Christ" comes from the Greek word for Messiah, the anointed king the prophets promised. That's the Christmas story. Thank you for walking through Advent with me.
